extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, patent examiners, and advanced law students in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evaluative criteria governing what may be patented in the United States, how patents must be written and prosecuted, and how validity, infringement, remedies, and related procedures are judged in law and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-Matter for which Letters-Patent may be granted
rubrics_metrics.description: What may be the subject-matter of letters-patent (p. 562 §6; p. 580 §3; p. 588 §11): must be new and useful; may be an art/process, a machine, a manufacture, or a composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates categories (machine, manufacture, composition of matter, process/art). Treatise explains differences between these categories and gives guidance about how the law treats each (e.g., machine vs process distinctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (First Inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is a statutory requisite; novelty of a process, composition, or machine is determined by whether the subject-matter was previously known or used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests for novelty vary by subject-matter. Prior printed publication, prior patent, or prior public use can defeat novelty. Foreign prior uses and intermediate abandonment are treated with nuance. Lack of novelty renders a patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / Usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention must be useful — twofold meaning: (1) not injurious; (2) capable of practical application. Utility is a test of invention; want of utility is equivalent to want of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluates practical utility; a useless claimed part will not be fatal if the machine as a whole is useful, but claiming what inventor knows to be useless is fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention: Qualities and Position
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention is decided by the character of the result, not merely amount of ingenuity; must be more than frivolous change; amount of 'thought' needed discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise discusses tests (result-orientation), degree of invention required, and evidentiary matters for proving invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles vs Patentable Application
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract principle or mere scientific discovery, disconnected from a mode of application, is not patentable; a claim for an abstract principle or for an abstract result apart from means is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A principle may be patented only insofar as it is embodied in or applied by particular means; claim for principle apart from means prevents subsequent invention and is invalid. The treatise outlines requisites when a principle may be claimed and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity or Diversity of Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on whether one patent may cover more than one invention; whether a single patent can validly cover a whole machine and also its parts, or two distinct inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One patent may cover related aspects but cannot validly cover two distinct inventions; discussion of 'unity' and classification of machines into classes to determine scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of Principle / Scope of Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent (claim) cannot be more extensive than the invention; claims are construed together with the specification, and cannot cover what is merely well-known or an abstract principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are construed liberally but limited to the disclosed invention; courts interpret claim scope in light of specification and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification: Required Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must disclose the inventor's best knowledge, describe the invention sufficiently, enable skilled workmen to apply it without making inventive efforts, include necessary steps, and be attested; drawings when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification's object: present subject-matter clearly and distinguish old from new. It must tell how to remove injurious matter, state where unusual ingredients may be obtained, and set variable proportions. Omission of essential matter is fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of Specification (Enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency is judged by whether the description enables persons skilled in the art to make and use the invention without inventive effort; sufficiency is a question for the jury under proper instructions and for the court in construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court and jury roles explained. The specification need not explain what is well-known; it must not omit any step that facilitates practice. False statements or withheld parts of knowledge render patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: Purpose and Drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim's object is to ascertain what is claimed as new (not to aid the description); it must be clear, distinguish the new from the old, and not be broader than the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may be a means of clearly presenting subject-matter; while clumsy wording may sometimes cover both product and process, defective or imperfectly worded claims can defeat a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission from the Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of what is essential from the specification is fatal; omission that affects only degree of benefit may not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examines whether omitted matter is essential to enable practice; omission of an ingredient or step that is essential will invalidate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Use and Printed Publication as Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior public use or prior printed publication of the invention destroys the right to patent; what constitutes public use and publication depends on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctions between single use subsequently abandoned, place (foreign vs domestic), and what counts as publication. Publication and public use are ordinarily jury questions; in law, courts decide their legal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patents / Prior Public Work
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior patent or prior public work that contains a full and clear description can defeat a later patent; a mere hint is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To defeat later claims, prior patents must themselves be full and clear. The treatise explains evidence required to show prior art anticipates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue and Amendment of Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue is permitted to correct errors; new patent upon surrender presumed to be for same invention; reissue may be used to amend specification/claims under limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue allowed when original patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of defective specification or claim; reissue cannot be used to enlarge claim scope improperly. Surrender and reissue effects discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment and Intermediate Abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment of an invention or intermediate abandonment can affect patent rights; a single subsequent abandoned use does not necessarily defeat patent but may in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether abandonment defeats patent depends on whether there was a complete invention prior to patentee's claim and the nature of the subsequent use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment, Recording, and Title
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment of patents and rights must be executed and recorded; rules when recording is necessary and effect of assignment on ownership and suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise explains how assignments are made, when they should be recorded, and legal consequences for rights and standing to sue. Joint ownership and assignment nuances covered elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Invention / Joint Inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for joint inventive contributions: joint invention can be patented; effect of separate patents on subsequent joint patent; whether one co-inventor may take out letters in his own name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses rights of joint inventors, treatment of subsequent patents, and ability of one co-inventor to sue or obtain patents alone; see assignment/joint ownership rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee vs Assignee: Rights and Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between a licensee and an assignee; the extent to which a licensee is estopped, whether apportionable, whether licensee can recover royalties paid, and whether they can withhold payments after patent declared invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains limits on licensee's remedies and defenses; a licensee who continues to use may be estopped from challenging validity; details on consequences of contract violation and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of Patent / Duration and Extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms of letters-patent and rules for how long granted, virtual extension to 16 (19) years in context of earlier statutes, distinction between renewal and reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical statutory treatment explained; treatise describes calculations of term, effect of reissue/surrender on term, and differences between renewal and reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Tests for Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement defined for machines, manufactures, compositions and processes; how infringement occurs (use, making, selling) and when sale of product/materials constitutes or does not constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details on infringement by use vs sale, the role of equivalents, whether sale of products of a patented machine is infringement (generally not per se), and when material sales implicate infringement. Tests and examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical Equivalents Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine addressing whether devices or processes practically attaining the same result by substantially the same means infringe (mechanical equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may pass on use of mechanical equivalents; treatise covers tests, examples, scope, and limits to the equivalents doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair vs Reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawful owner of a patented machine may repair it (not an infringement) but reconstruction that makes a new article is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses distinction, examples, and factors courts consider to decide whether acts are permissible repair or impermissible reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of Products / Materials and Infringement Liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of articles made by a patented machine is not per se an infringement; sale of the materials of a patented machine is generally not infringement unless connected with use of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendor liability may arise if vendor is connected with the infringing use. Sales to agent used for detection are not per se infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies at Law: Damages and Profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for recovery of damages and profits for infringement; calculation principles and evidentiary presumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise sets out burden of proof (patentee to show infringement and damages), rule of damages, and when profits may be awarded; statutory and common-law considerations discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies in Equity: Injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable remedies to restrain infringements, including injunctions, principles for granting equitable relief, and interplay with actions at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when injunctive relief is appropriate, interlocutory vs permanent, and ancillary equitable remedies; discusses jurisdictional and procedural aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings and Notice Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularity required in pleadings and notices (e.g., in pleading general issue, defendant must particularize and specify which parts of patent are attacked).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must specify parts of the patent to be attacked; evidence of general state of the art need not always be furnished in notice. The treatise explains specific pleading forms and consequences of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and Burden of Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocation of burdens: defendant must show want of novelty; patentee must show infringement and sufficiency of specification; oath at application is prima facie evidence of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details the types of evidence admissible (prior use, printed work, patents), role of witnesses and experts, and how courts and juries weigh evidence. Presumptions from grants are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions of Law vs Questions of Fact (Court and Jury Roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes issues for the court (e.g., claim construction) from those for the jury (e.g., sufficiency under proper instructions, novelty in some contexts), and how judges should instruct juries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise provides guidance on dividing questions (construction of patent and specification for the court; factual determinations like public use and enablement for the jury) and appropriate instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and Venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope of jurisdiction: jurisdiction of Congress, original and appellate jurisdiction of Circuit, District and Supreme Courts; federal courts' exclusivity and limits (contracts vs patent matters); where suits must be brought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains which courts have jurisdiction over patent suits, venue rules, effect of personal jurisdiction (right to enjoin violations in other districts), and appellate limitations (e.g., costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of Patents and Interfering Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures and grounds by which patents may be repealed or set aside and treatment of interfering patents (prior conflicting patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details remedies to annul patents, grounds (lack of novelty, insufficiency, fraud), and how interfering patents are handled in litigation and administrative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath in Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Application oath (or affirmation) accompanies application; its form, effects, and role as prima facie evidence of novelty; irregularities cured by grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form variations and statutory changes noted. Oath's evidentiary value and consequences of irregularities (often cured by grant) are explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process vs Machine Distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between a process (art) and a machine; a process is a manufacture under English statute; a machine-patent does not necessarily cover the process and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise gives tests for novelty in processes, when product and process may be claimed together, and limits on claiming process as improvement of machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of Ingredients in Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of new for old ingredients in a process producing a beneficial result can be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examines when substitution constitutes invention (useful, non-trivial substitution leading to beneficial result) and when mere change of material is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of Patentee as Inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that the patentee is the inventor; evidence can rebut this presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in disputes about priority or ownership; treatise describes evidence that shifts burdens on this presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule on Claims for Useless Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a useless part is not fatal if the machine as a whole is useful; but claiming what patentee knows to be useless is fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examines inventors' knowledge and the practical usefulness of claimed elements in context of entire invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict and Cure of Defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Verdict may cure defects in declaration (pleading) under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when verdicts cure formal defects and the limits of verdict-based cures for substantive defects.
